title: Prefill vs Decode Pipeline: Design Draft (overlap, micro-batching, stream priorities)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working design doc exploring the prefill vs decode pipeline trade-offs for the serving runtime. Focus areas: overlap opportunities, micro-batching strategies, stream priority semantics, scheduler changes, KV-cache interactions, and kernel implications. Goal is to pick a pragmatic architecture that meets our latency SLOs for streaming decodes while preserving throughput/cost targets for prefill-heavy workloads.

Context / motivation:
- We currently treat prefill (long context token generation and kv-cache population) and decode (autoregressive streaming) as mostly separate execution paths.
- Increasing demand for simultaneous streaming sessions + high concurrency batched prefill jobs causes resource contention, increasing tail latency for live streams.
- Improved overlap and micro-batching can reduce wasted GPU cycles and improve utilization, but naive batching can hurt streaming tails.

Design goals:
- Prioritize interactive streaming decodes to meet 95th/99th latency SLOs (< 250ms per token target for typical routes)
- Maintain high aggregate throughput for prefill workloads (batch-friendly) to keep per-token cost low
- Allow smart overlap: reuse prefills' KV cache state when safe, and avoid redundant work when a stream upgrades from prefill to decode
- Keep kernel selection deterministic per request characteristics (seq_len, model variant, quantization) to avoid repeated re-compilation cost
- Be incremental: propose a path compatible with Dedicated/Private deployments and minimal control-plane changes

Terminology:
- prefill: initial forward pass to encode prompt tokens and populate KV cache for subsequent decode steps
- decode: autoregressive token generation steps (streaming) that read/write KV cache per step
- micro-batching: grouping small decode steps across concurrent streams into batches to amortize kernel cost
- overlap: executing prefill and decode concurrently on same GPU when safe and beneficial

Options considered (high level):
1) Strict separation (current): distinct pipelines for prefill and decode, separate queues and resources. Simple but leads to underutilized GPUs and stream stalls when prefill floods the machine.
2) Unified overlapped pipeline: single scheduler + prioritized queues that allow interleaving prefill and decode ops on the same device with preemption and micro-batching. More complex but higher utilization.
3) Hybrid: keep dedicated fast-path for low-latency decode on a small portion of capacity (hot lane) + background prefill pool that shares remaining capacity.

Recommendation (hybrid -> move to unified once stable):
Short term: implement a 'hot-lane' decode priority that pins a fraction of GPU slots for streaming decodes (configurable per pool) and leaves the rest for prefill/batch. This reduces risk while improving streaming tails.
Medium term: implement a unified prioritized scheduler supporting micro-batching, preemption, and cache-awareness to safely overlap prefill and decode on the same device.

Scheduler design (unified):
- Queues: maintain at least three logical queues per device: HIGH (interactive streaming decodes), MEDIUM (prefill/batched requests that are latency-sensitive but not streaming), LOW (background evals, bulk embedding jobs).
- Admission: requests labeled as streaming decode get HIGH priority. Prefills and large batches start in MEDIUM. A health metric (device load, memory headroom) gates admission to HIGH/MEDIUM.
- Micro-batching window: for HIGH queue, use a very short accumulation window (W_high = 1-4ms) to form micro-batches of decode steps; for MEDIUM use W_med = 8-30ms to create larger batches. Windows adapt to arrival rate to avoid hurting streaming.
- Batch keying: only batch ops with compatible kernel parameters: same model variant, same dtype/quantization, same layer execution step (e.g. self-attention forward for same layer index), and compatible seq_len (or pad to next power-of-two cost model).
- Fairness & starvation prevention: enforce weighted fairness so MEDIUM isn't starved; if MEDIUM queue latency > threshold (configurable) for X seconds, temporarily boost MEDIUM.
- Preemption model: allow HIGH micro-batches to preempt a running MEDIUM batch at layer boundaries where kernel state is consistent (we can checkpoint minimal state). Preemption points must be performance cheap; plan: preempt only between layers or after attention blocks where stream consistency maintained.

KV-cache semantics and overlap:
- Cache ownership: KV cache is per-session (route + model + session_id) and lives in GPU memory; both prefill and decode operations read/write the same KV object.
- Warm-up reuse: when prefill and decode are separated in time, avoid recomputing prefill if KV cache is present and valid. The scheduler should prefer routing to the GPU that already holds the KV shard.
- Consistency and partial prefills: support partial prefill merge — if a user sends a chunked prompt (e.g., streaming prompt ingestion), we allow incremental prefill that populates the cache and immediately enables decode micro-batching.
- Cache eviction: implement LRU per-GPU with prioritization: mark active streaming sessions as protected from eviction; background jobs are evicted first. Expose soft memory thresholds and spill-to-host fallback.

Micro-batching strategy for decode streaming:
- Token-step batching: collect decode steps from multiple sessions and execute in a single kernel with per-item offsets. Maintain per-step latency timer to avoid holding a token wait longer than SLO.
- Max micro-batch size heuristic: limit to N_high (e.g., 16-32) for LOW-latency streams; adapt based on measured per-token latency vs throughput curves.
- Bucketization: bucket streams by current token index modulo small power-of-two to increase alignment for KV access patterns and reduce memory striding overhead.

Kernel & compilation considerations:
- Kernel re-use: minimize JIT/compilation noise by designing stable kernel keys that include quantization, batch dims, and seq_len range buckets. Avoid per-request unique keys.
- Fused kernels for streaming: prefer kernels that fuse attention + KV read/write when possible to reduce memory traffic in streaming hot-path.
- Layer-boundary preemption requires deterministic kernel boundaries. Favor kernels that finish at layer boundaries to enable safe preempt.

Resource accounting and cost model:
- Meter streaming tokens separately from prefill tokens (different cost weight) to reflect SLO priority and to charge customers correctly for hot-lane usage.
- Track GPU occupancy vs effective tokens processed to compute opportunity cost of preempts. Use these metrics for autoscaler decisions and capacity planning.

Edge cases and safety:
- Model fallback: if preemptions cause too many small replays, fallback to strict separation for that session.
- Host fallback on memory pressure: if KV cannot be held on GPU for a session, route to host-based KV with higher latency but avoid OOM.
- Multi-model shard conflicts: avoid co-locating incompatible model variants that force different kernel configs unless necessary.

Open questions / experiments to run:
1) Micro-batch window sensitivity: run A/B with W_high=[1,4,8]ms across traffic mixes to find break-even point for 95/99 latency vs throughput.
2) Preemption cost: measure actual time to preempt at layer boundaries on our common models (Llama2-Chat, MPT, etc.).
3) KV locality benefits: quantify latency improvement when routing decode to GPUs that already hold KV shards vs cold route.
4) Hot-lane sizing: determine % of cluster to reserve for hot-lane to reach 99th token latency SLO under realistic traffic patterns.

Implementation plan & milestones:
- Spike (2w): prototype unified scheduler in local harness with simulated request mixes. Implement micro-batching window timers and simple priority queues. Measure baseline.
- Hot-lane pilot (3w): implement hot-lane config and reserve slots for streaming in one dedicated pool; deploy to canary cluster.
- Unified scheduler (6w): implement preemption at layer boundaries, KV-aware routing, and kernel batch-key matching. Add metrics/alerts.
- Rollout (4w): gradual traffic migration, rollback flags, and guardrails (max preempt frequency, per-session fallback).

Action items / next steps:
- Ethan: run initial micro-batch window sensitivity spike (start 2026-03-02).
- Ava: draft scheduler/queue API for inclusion in runtime agent by 2026-03-09.
- Ravi & Noah: benchmark preemption cost on representative models and upload results to linked_artifacts.
- Team: review cost metering proposal with finance for hot-lane pricing.

Notes / informal observations:
- Real traffic has bursts where prefill floods on product release days; a hybrid approach gives us a practical quick fix.
- Developers prefer deterministic behavior: avoid reactive kernel recompilation on common production paths.
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: aim for incremental rollout and observable guardrails.

References:
- see linked_artifacts above for PRs and conf pages.
- internal perf spreadsheet: "prefill-decode-benchmarks-2026-02.csv" (in Drive, eng-serving-runtime folder).

Open questions to discuss in next design review:
- Should we expose a customer-level hint to mark sessions as "historic-heavy-prefill" vs "interactive" to help routing?
- What SLA tiers automatically get hot-lane priority vs pay-for-priority model?

End of draft.

[notes-to-self] This doc is a working draft — expect edits, missing micro-bench numbers will be filled in after initial spike.
